title: Starting Solid Foods
hook: Most babies are ready for their first solid foods at around six months — alongside continued breast milk or formula, not instead of it.
key_points: Guidelines commonly suggest introducing solids around 6 months, when babies can sit with support and hold their head steady.
Milk (breast or formula) stays the main source of nutrition through the first year; solids are added on top.
Introducing common allergens like peanut and egg early (in age-appropriate forms) may lower allergy risk for many babies.
Avoid choking hazards (whole nuts, grapes, hard chunks); honey is not safe before 12 months due to infant botulism risk.
content_html: Starting solids is a milestone, but it's an addition rather than a switch. For most babies, around six months is the sweet spot — by then they can typically sit with support, hold their head steady, and show interest in food. Crucially, breast milk or formula remains the main source of nutrition through the whole first year; early solids are about practice, taste, and texture as much as calories.
extra_html: Current guidance from bodies like the AAP also encourages introducing common allergenic foods — such as smooth peanut butter and well-cooked egg, in age-appropriate textures — relatively early, which may reduce the chance of developing those allergies. At the same time, steer clear of choking hazards like whole nuts, whole grapes, and hard chunks, and remember that honey is not safe before the first birthday because of the risk of infant botulism. This is general information; your pediatrician can advise on your baby's readiness and any allergy considerations.

related.title: Breastfeeding and Formula Both Feed a Baby Well
related.hook: Health bodies recommend breastfeeding where possible, but properly prepared infant formula is a safe, nourishing alternative — a fed baby is the goal.

related.title: Why Breastfed Babies Need Vitamin D Drops
related.hook: Breast milk is nearly perfect — but it's low in vitamin D. Pediatricians recommend a daily 400 IU vitamin D supplement for every breastfed and partly breastfed baby, starting in the first days.

flashcards.prompt: Around what age are most babies ready to start solid foods?
flashcards.explanation_html: Around 6 months most babies can sit with support and hold their head steady — signs of readiness. Milk stays the main nutrition source until age 1.

flashcards.prompt: Which of these is unsafe to give a baby under 12 months?
flashcards.explanation_html: Honey can carry spores that cause infant botulism in babies under one year. It becomes safe after the first birthday.

flashcards.prompt: Do solid foods replace milk in the first year?
flashcards.back_html: No. Breast milk or formula stays the main source of nutrition through the first year; solids are introduced on top of milk, not instead of it.
